answer.label: Not Nelson Mandela — actually Marianne Williamson
answer.sourceLine: These words are from Marianne Williamson’s 1992 book A Return to Love ↗ (Chapter 7). The passage is one of the internet’s most persistent misattributions: it is routinely credited to Nelson Mandela’s 1994 inaugural address, but Mandela never spoke or wrote it — and Williamson herself has repeatedly said so.

source.heading: The real source

docMeta.dd: A Return to Love: Reflections on the Principles of A Course in Miracles
Nelson Mandela (falsely tied to his 1994 inauguration)

source.excerpt: Our deepest fear is not that we are inadequate. Our deepest fear is that we are powerful beyond measure. It is our light, not our darkness, that most frightens us. We ask ourselves, ‘Who am I to be brilliant, gorgeous, talented, fabulous?’ Actually, who are you not to be? … And as we let our own light shine, we unconsciously give other people permission to do the same. As we are liberated from our own fear, our presence automatically liberates others.
trail: Marianne Williamson wrote the passage in her 1992 debut A Return to Love, Chapter 7 ↗, per Quote Investigator’s tracing.
The Nelson Mandela attribution surfaced publicly by 1998, when The New York Times noted commencement speakers ↗ quoting it as Mandela’s words — “Problem is, Mr. Mandela never said it.”
A 2019 fact-check ↗ rated the Mandela attribution False, citing the Mandela Foundation’s 2007 correction.

author.bio: Marianne Williamson (b. 1952) is an American author and spiritual teacher best known for interpreting A Course in Miracles. Her 1992 debut, A Return to Love, became a #1 New York Times bestseller after she appeared on Oprah Winfrey’s show. She has repeatedly clarified that the widely shared “deepest fear” passage is hers, not Nelson Mandela’s.

misattribution.heading: The Mandela myth
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most famous misattributions on the internet — feel-good, empowering, and endlessly pinned on Nelson Mandela.

items.why: The passage is commonly said to come from Mandela’s 1994 presidential inauguration, but it appears in none of his three public addresses at that time ↗. In 1998 The New York Times flagged commencement speakers — including Hillary Clinton and Mae Jemison — quoting it as Mandela’s: “Problem is, Mr. Mandela never said it.”

misattribution.truthLine: The words are Marianne Williamson’s, from A Return to Love (1992) ↗; Williamson and the Nelson Mandela Foundation have both said Mandela never uttered them.

context.heading: Why it stuck to Mandela
lead: The passage is a near-perfect “magnet quote”: uplifting, quotable, and built for graduation speeches and inspirational posters. Attaching it to Nelson Mandela — a globally revered figure emerging from prison to the presidency — gave it borrowed gravity it never needed.

Marianne Williamson has been gracious about the mix-up, writing that she would have been honored had Mandela quoted her, but that he did not. The correction is now backed by the Nelson Mandela Foundation itself.
context.pull: “Problem is, Mr. Mandela never said it.”
